item.title: Managing Caregiver Grief
item.description:
Caregiving

Managing Caregiver Grief

How to handle grief and isolation while caring for a loved one.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Caregiver grief is a common experience.
  • Avoiding judgment about feelings is important.
  • Sharing feelings between caregiver and care receiver brings them closer.
  • Social supports, including caregiver support groups, help normalize grief.

The main reason that Willa isolated herself while caring for her disabled husband, Dan, who was paralyzed from a massive stroke, was that she was afraid all her emotions would spill out if anyone asked her how she was doing. It was easier for her to buck up and face her long, difficult days without “going there.” But as the months of caregiving became years, Willa began to find she could no longer control her feelings.

When a police officer pulled her over after she’d rolled through a stop sign, she began to cry and couldn’t stop. He became so frustrated that he just gave her a warning, but even then, she couldn’t stop wailing. A dam had broken. It took her a half hour to calm down enough to go home and appear composed for Dan.

On another occasion, when Dan spilled water all over himself, she watched herself blow it out of proportion, unable to stop berating him for being so clumsy. Later when she was calmer, she apologized to him again and again but felt she’d never forgive herself for yelling at him.

Like many caregivers, Willa felt overwhelmed by the intensity of her complex emotions. She also felt tremendously ashamed about being overwhelmed, as if she should be stronger. The hardest among her feelings to manage was a deep sadness that would come up suddenly. She was struggling with a variety of types of grief.

She was feeling “anticipatory grief,” the most common kind during caregiving, in which the caregiver is grieving the future loss of the loved one, knowing that he or she is eventually going to die from their condition. Often, caregivers want to hide these feelings from their care receiver, but the sadness can be so heavy that it begins to affect the caregiver’s physical and emotional functioning. It doesn’t end until their loved one passes away.

Willa was also experiencing what psychologist Pauline Boss has termed “ambiguous loss,” in which the person being grieved is still physically present but cognitively absent, such as when a care recipient has advanced dementia. As Boss has pointed out, these are especially stressful situations for caregivers because they feel caught between grieving the person who can no longer relate to them as they once did and still caring for that person who is very much present.

There’s also grief that is invisible, sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” in which the caregiver experiences the loss of her hopes and dreams for the future with her care recipient, as well as mourning the changing balance of what used to be a relationship of equal partners to one of caregiver and care recipient. That changed balance often means decreased communication and physical intimacy between them. These losses are often not spoken about and are hidden from friends and family.

If a caregiver has to give up or reduce work and social occasions to be with their care recipient, then she can feel grief around the loss of her career, social circles, imagined future, and life goals. She can feel weighed down by the burden of all she has to do. Her sense of identity and independence may be imperiled.

When Willa came to see us for psychotherapy, we offered her a few important ways to manage her overwhelming grief. We hope these suggestions will be helpful to other caregivers, too:

  1. We provided psychoeducation about how common grief is among caregivers in order to help her understand that her feelings were normal. This helped her feel less ashamed about her reactions to caregiving
  2. We reinforced this message by asking her to share her grief feelings with us without censoring them or judging herself. We then listened closely and validated her emotions as she cried and talked about her losses, her loneliness, and her horror at Dan’s horrible circumstances. Since the day he had his stroke, she told us, she’d never stopped grieving for him and for herself.
  3. We recommended that she not try to protect her husband by hiding all her grief from him because his paralyzed state was a constant, glaring reminder to both of them of how trapped and sad each of them felt. We noted that efforts at protection by limiting communication only made them feel more distant from each other.
  4. We discussed the importance of finding a way to strengthen their connection with one another to develop a greater feeling of communion, provide mutual solace, and feel more like a team facing his disability together. We then gave her some ideas for how to have an initial conversation with him by starting small and just acknowledging to each other that these were hard times about which they both felt very sad.
  5. We recommended that Willa increase her social supports in other ways, including joining a caregiver support group in which other caregivers would be able to validate her feelings, too. After a few months of processing her grief feelings in therapy and gaining more control over them, we also suggested she try reconnecting with friends she’d isolated herself from in order to share with them a bit about what she was going through.

Therapy didn’t take away Willa’s grief feelings. To the contrary, it helped her become more aware of them and their impact on her overall behavior. But understanding and accepting those feelings through therapy made what were overwhelming emotions more bearable, brought her closer to her husband and friends, and helped her be less hard on herself.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: The Power of Empathy in Medicine and Self-Care
item.description:
Chronic Illness

The Power of Empathy in Medicine and Self-Care

Treat yourself with care when navigating the isolation of chronic illness.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Measuring medical outcomes based on doctor warmth and conveyed empathy.
  • Compassionate care as an effective medical treatment, it's not just bedside manner.
  • We can’t always guarantee empathetic doctors, but we can practice self-compassion ourselves.

In the last month, I’ve been absorbed in Meghan O'Rourke’s insightful book, The Invisible Kingdom: Reimagining Chronic Illness. It examines the often dark and misconstrued world of long-term health conditions, specifically intangible illnesses that manage to slip under the diagnostic radar for many years. But she addresses all medical conditions that typically take a huge toll on our psychological well-being.

The author clarifies the maddening reality faced by millions: existing with often incapacitating physical symptoms, while average blood work, routine scans, and conventional diagnostic testing continuously come back completely normal or at unalarming levels that don’t raise a medical eyebrow. It is a prevailing work that speaks directly to the experience of being trapped in the limbo of unseen illness, where the body clearly conveys that something is wrong; yet the outdated medical system lacks the tools—sometimes even the desire—to recognize it.

Among the many fascinating concepts introduced is the "Care Effect." This refers to studies that measure medical outcomes based directly on the degree of warmth, consideration, sincere care, and human compassion a doctor shows a patient. Predictably, the data show that patients cared for by empathetic, friendlier physicians fare significantly better than those treated by detached ones. Researchers are beginning to view this approach not just as an agreeable bedside manner, but as an authentic therapeutic intervention capable of driving noticeable healing across all types of illness. For many, it is sometimes equivalent to medication.

Feeling genuine respect, empathy, and active listening—particularly while circumnavigating a confusing health crisis—can provide quantifiable relief, whether a sickness is formally diagnosed or remains an unexplained mystery.

A colossal toll

The book also delves into the colossal emotional toll of long-term illness. Living with a chronic condition slowly corrodes a person's self-esteem and sense of identity. It is easy to lose sight of your strengths and value when you begin to define yourself exclusively by a diagnosis. When you add the irritation of being disbelieved or turned away by doctors, family, and friends, the loneliness can feel overwhelming.

As a mental health professional, I have always understood the need to offer kindness and unconditional positive regard to all my clients. Yet, reflecting on the care effect made me realize how central that equal level of clinical empathy is in the medical field—specifically for individuals enduring the silent, draining weight of chronic illness.

In her book, O'Rourke recounts her difficult, multi-year trials of living with baffling symptoms. Having recently been diagnosed with an unspecified autoimmune condition myself, her chronicle resounded profoundly with me. Reading her narrative felt universal. I felt less unique.

A central thread in O'Rourke’s story is the reprieve that came with symptom identification. Establishing those medical verdicts offered no immediate resolution—her chronic circumstances remain lifelong—yet the transparency provided instantaneous validation. Having names for what she was enduring confirmed her struggles, changing how she approached handling her daily symptoms. However, the true game-changer was the authentication of her suffering. Although it didn’t prompt taking a victory lap, it marked an epic shift in her expedition to get well.

This highlights a key point: while we cannot always guarantee we’ll find sincere, empathetic doctors with excellent bedside manner (most of the time we won’t), we can direct the philosophies of the care effect inward for ourselves. For example, I can teach myself to extend that same consideration and unconditional kindness to myself, even if it feels weird at first. It requires active vigilance to notice when my inner critic is dominating my thoughts—because that internal judgment can be unrelenting sometimes. Ultimately, learning about the care effect as a therapeutic tool for others served as a commanding wake-up call: it is an intervention we all need to practice regularly. Regardless of whether or not you are presently suffering from a chronic illness, and/or if it's identifiable or not.

The gray area of medical vagueness

If you are currently navigating the grueling terrain of a chronic condition, your pain, fatigue, worry, and frustration are real, regardless of whether a standard lab test or blood panel picks it up. Residing in the gray area of medical vagueness can make you question your own experience, but the absence of diagnostic proof does not invalidate what you are feeling. You know your body better than anyone else. No one can take that away from you.

As you probe for answers and advocate for healthcare providers who truly listen and validate your experience, withholding gentleness from yourself hurts. It is easy to become your own detractor when your body doesn't perform the way it used to. Offer yourself the understanding that is missing from the skepticism you are used to.

Start practicing your own internal care effect today. Give yourself explicit consent to rest without culpability, respect the daily limits your body sets, and actively challenge the inner critic that insists you should be doing more. The adage is true: "True healing isn't about closing a chapter; it's about learning to live with the story." And learning to give yourself compassion for the story.

item.title: Do You Distance Regulate in Your Relationships?
item.description:
Relationships

Do You Distance Regulate in Your Relationships?

How we use distance to manage intimacy.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Distance can be physical, emotional, or mental, even when we are physically together.
  • Distance can help us manage feelings we aren't always aware of or able to express.
  • For some gay men, privacy and distance can become ways of protecting themselves in relationships.
Source: Ahbsek Rai / Unsplash

When I was an associate marriage and family therapist, a common theme that would continue to appear in my client case presentations during supervision was distance regulation.

At the time, I hadn’t heard of the term. It wasn’t something I learned about in graduate school. But the more clients I began working with, the more distance regulation became a common theme.

Whether it was in individual or couples therapy, people would often seek therapy because of communication challenges in their relationships.

In the process of learning their history, I would tune into patterns, how people responded, whether a partner was hyper- or hypo-aroused, and I would begin to identify their defenses. I learned that what could look maladaptive in someone’s current life was often a coping strategy they adopted early on to take care of themselves.

Distance regulation is a concept to describe how people manage the amount of space they have in their relationships. It can be physical, emotional, or even mental. For some people, creating distance is an important way of managing how they feel.

Physical distance is the most obvious, but distance can also happen emotionally, when we withhold our feelings, or mentally, when we check out, even when we are physically together. I see this with clients who describe sitting together on the couch watching television while one person is on his phone and the other feels alone.

The behavior itself doesn't necessarily mean someone is distance regulating. Before assigning a label, I try to be curious about what is happening for each person.

Some people might not even be aware of how they feel, so using distance can help regulate their nervous system. On the other hand, a person might be acutely aware of how they feel; however, it’s difficult to express it to their partner, friends, or loved ones, and space serves as a way to communicate an emotion they’re unable to verbalize otherwise.

Communication researcher Jon Hess developed a model for distance regulation in personal relationships that describes the different ways people create and manage distance. Other research has examined the ongoing tension between intimacy, vulnerability, and distance, and the ways people manage their needs for connection and autonomy.

Even though it's a pretty common, and easily understood, way of managing ourselves, there isn't much out there in the way of articles, podcasts, or books that explains what distance regulation can look like or why someone might develop it in the first place. I wanted to write something I could share with clients, as well as something clinicians could use when they encounter distance regulation in their clinical work.

Distance Regulation in Relationships

A person may need time alone after spending time with other people. They may need physical space from a partner or less communication when their nervous system, unbeknownst to them, is activated. They may also create distance when a relationship becomes more intimate or vulnerable.

For partners, this can create a difficult dynamic. The person creating distance may be trying to regulate himself, while his partner experiences his distance as rejection or avoidance. The result can be conflict, particularly when neither person understands what’s driving the behavior.

Learning where our defenses come from can change how we respond to them. Like skin, defenses are there to protect us. We don't want to just rip them off. When we understand why we developed certain ways of taking care of ourselves, we can find more ways to manage intimacy and communicate our need for physical or emotional space.

Gay Men’s Relationship to Distance

Distance regulation isn't unique to gay men, and not all gay men distance regulate. Many gay men, however, grow up learning that privacy and distance can be ways of protecting themselves, which can later become part of how they manage relationships.

For some gay men, hiding parts of ourselves begins when we’re young. We learn to monitor what we say, how we act, what we like, and who we have crushes on. We pay attention to what feels safe to share and what doesn't.

For some men, creating distance later in life can serve a similar purpose. Independence can feel safer than depending on someone else. Having time alone can make it easier to feel like ourselves when intimacy becomes vulnerable.

Distance itself isn't always a problem. We all have different needs for privacy, autonomy, solitude, and connection. The question is whether distance has become the primary way a person knows how to manage himself in relationships.

How do you manage distance? Do you find yourself needing to take a break from people or your partner, but judging it as something bad?

Finding balance is key, and distance is no different. Whether you need physical, emotional, or mental distance, communicating your needs while also paying attention to the needs of the people in your life can help you have compassion for yourself when you need space.

item.title: The Unseen Aspects of the Female Archetypes of "The Odyssey"
item.description:
Gender

The Unseen Aspects of the Female Archetypes of "The Odyssey"

In "The Odyssey" film, female characters are rendered hollow and one-dimensional.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • In reality, no person is completely good or bad.
  • Humans are a blend of flaws and virtues, and this inherent duality makes characters real and resonant.
  • Ancient Greek lore is rich with complex female archetypes who embody vices and virtues.
  • Unfortunately, the female movie characters, like Penelope, Athena, and Circe, feel severely underdeveloped.

Christopher Nolan’s new adaptation of The Odyssey created a powerful portal of resonance for audiences, sparking a global obsession with Greek mythology. However, despite its three-hour runtime, Odysseus is the only character explored in his full depth. He is the most complex and psychologically realistic figure in the epic, as he is portrayed as flawed. He is a multi-faceted, nuanced, and layered hero struggling with his own inherent darkness. His strength and cleverness are constantly balanced by his pride, weakness, and vulnerability. Psychologically, his 20-year journey home represents the individuation process—the painful but necessary struggle to overcome temptation and confront the shadow self before emerging as “whole.”

While the film attempts to capture the grand scale of Greek mythology, it significantly flattens the psychological depth of its female characters. Ancient Greek lore is rich with complex female archetypes who embody a nuanced psychological blend of vices and virtues, light and darkness. Unfortunately, characters like Penelope, Athena, and Circe feel severely underdeveloped in this cinematic adaptation.(Take the Quiz + Find out Which Greek Myth Archetype Are You?).

Instead of portraying their intricate internal motivations, the film strips away their moral ambiguities and emotional conflicts. This portrayal misses a vital psychological truth: true strength lies in internal complexity, not just external status. In reality, no person is completely good or bad. Humans are a complicated blend of flaws and virtues, and this inherent duality makes characters real, interesting, and resonant.

The psychologist Heinz Kohut wrote that humans require three specific relationships in life to develop a cohesive self: idolization, twinship, and mirroring.

  • Idolization represents the gods, celebrities, and icons we look up to and idealize.
  • Twinship presents resonance—the deep feeling of connection with someone who shares
    our nature and experiences.
  • Mirroring represents those who look up to us with adoring eyes, confirming our sense of
    worth.

Consider the cinematic experience of Joker (2019). Audiences experienced a profound, soulful resonance with the main character portrayed by Joaquin Phoenix. It was deeply disturbing because he was warm, vulnerable, and relatable, yet simultaneously a villain. This duality created a perfect element of twinship.

Conversely, the traditional, seemingly perfect depiction of Superman—all virtue with no vice (except for a vulnerability to Kryptonite and an odd relationship with his mother)—fails to compete for this type of connection. No one cries for a flawless Superman; no one thinks about his internal world weeks later, because a character devoid of human flaws is hollow, one-dimensional, and unengaging.

We encounter this exact psychological failure in Nolan’s depiction of The Odyssey. The female characters are rendered as hollow, one-dimensional figures stripped of the essential element of twinship.

Penelope

In the movie, she is portrayed as the passive, long-suffering wife waiting helplessly in Ithaca, weeping over her loom, and serving as a static prize to be possessed or won back by Odysseus at the end of his journey. In reality, she had a brilliant strategic mind; her cunning was equal, if not sharper, than her husband's. She was known to be guarded and manipulative.

Though Nolan did depict her daily weaving and unweaving of the shroud as an active, deceptive act of psychological warfare against the suitors, there was more to her. She managed a collapsing kingdom under immense geopolitical pressure, demonstrating deep emotional resilience, skepticism, and calculating wisdom. When her husband finally returned, she tested his identity by ordering their immovable marital bed—built into a living olive tree—to be moved. She carefully observed his emotional distress; his outburst revealed that he held knowledge only Odysseus would know.

This trick proved that she is a master of cool intellect, a pragmatic strategist. She had a well-established pattern of balancing divine authority with a sharp, calculating understanding of human nature to protect her realm. This depth of character was lost in the movie, as even the servants knew she unraveled her tapestry nightly.

Athena

In the movie, the virgin goddess Athena is depicted as a guide who serves as Odysseus’s conscience, attempting to steer him back to the righteous path. In reality, she was much more complicated. In ancient lore, her patronage of Odysseus was never arbitrary. Instead, it represented a profound relationship of intellectual twinship; deeper dialogue, intellectual prowess, and sharp debate would have greatly enriched her on-screen character.

We can appreciate the complexity of her character in the myth of Medusa. Medusa was once a beautiful young maiden who dedicated her life to becoming a priestess under the guidance of Athena, the goddess of wisdom. Diligent and devoted, she aspired to emulate Athena’s life of virtue and celibacy.

One fateful day, Poseidon (God of the Sea) found Medusa in Athena’s sacred temple, where he viciously assaulted and raped her. In that harrowing moment, time seemed to freeze. Medusa inhaled the thick smoke of temple incense and caught sight of the waves lapping against the white-sand coastline, framed perfectly by the marble columns, as she stood paralyzed with fear. The virgin goddess Athena was outraged that her sacred temple had been desecrated by such a lewd act. However, instead of showing empathy toward Medusa or holding her uncle Poseidon accountable, she chose to punish Medusa.

Enraged, Athena transformed Medusa’s beautiful golden hair into writhing, venomous serpents. But that was not enough. As part of her curse, any man who dared to look into Medusa’s eyes was instantly petrified and turned into a stone statue, lost for all eternity. The once-fair maiden had been forever transformed into a grotesque creature, rejected by society and condemned to a life of solitude.

Ultimately, this brutal retribution exposes the deeply paradoxical nature of Athena’s personality, which seamlessly combined brilliant intellect with cold, unyielding calculation. Her complete lack of empathy for Medusa reveals a ruthless streak that fiercely prioritized her own divine pride and sacred status above all else. Behind her revered facade of wisdom lay a starkly unsympathetic figure, driven far more by rigid principles of control and institutional order than by genuine compassion. Again, like Odysseus, she is flawed, nuanced, and imperfect.

Circe

In the movie, she is portrayed as a powerful sorceress—the villainous witch leads Odysseus and his men astray by playing into their temptations. In reality, she was a formidable, independent goddess of sorcery and a complex archetype of female autonomy.

Circe’s transmutation of men into beasts represents a profound commentary on human nature and the regression of base impulses. Far from being a simple villain, she becomes an essential mentor to Odysseus after he earns her respect, providing him with critical esoteric knowledge, prophetic navigation advice for the Underworld, and the keys to surviving his future trials. However, in the movie, she is presented as another monster to be escaped.

item.title: When Defiance Began to Mean Something Else
item.description:
Child Development

When Defiance Began to Mean Something Else

A former student changed how I think about disruptive behavior.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • A diagnosis should never replace careful psychological assessment of a student's behavior.
  • Patterns such as cruelty, manipulation, and lack of remorse deserve closer attention.
  • Early understanding may help schools identify students who need more specialized intervention.
Source: Pexels-Cottonbro

More than 20 years have passed, and I still remember Juan Manuel. I have changed his name and details to protect his identity.

Juan Manuel was in 11th grade when I met him at a school in Bogotá. Before we ever spoke, I already knew who he was. Teachers mentioned him during staff meetings. Students talked about him in the hallways. His name surfaced so often that I assumed I was about to meet another teenager who constantly challenged authority, and that seemed to be exactly the case.

Juan Manuel had been diagnosed with oppositional defiant disorder (ODD). He questioned almost every instruction, argued with teachers, and rarely accepted responsibility for what he did. If something happened in the classroom, someone else usually received the blame. None of those behaviors surprised me. By then, I had already worked with many adolescents whose behavior created daily conflict at school.

It was everything else that caught my attention.

Teachers told me that several chickens kept on the school grounds had been found dead. Students reported seeing Juan Manuel hurting lizards during recess. I heard complaints about stray dogs that wandered near the school. Nobody seemed able to explain why those incidents were happening. Neither could I.

One afternoon I watched another student walk away from an interaction with Juan Manuel in tears. I remember standing there, almost expecting some reaction. Maybe an apology, a look of regret, or even a moment of discomfort. Instead, I saw an expression that I have never forgotten. I left school that afternoon thinking about one question: Was it more than ODD?

When a Diagnosis Is No Longer Enough

Over the years, I had met many adolescents who argued with adults, reacted impulsively, and resisted authority. Those behaviors certainly created challenges for families and schools, but they were familiar to me. Juan Manuel raised different concerns.

During recess, he sometimes entered the classroom while everyone else was outside. He opened classmates' backpacks without permission and searched through their belongings. Pens, sharpeners, and small personal items disappeared. When teachers confronted him, he denied taking anything, even when other students had seen him doing so.

His classmates gradually learned to avoid him. Some feared becoming his next target. Others tried not to attract his attention. Teachers responded with different disciplinary strategies, but very little changed.

As my work in forensic psychology continued, I often thought about students like Juan Manuel. When I later revisited the scientific literature, one finding immediately stood out. Most children and adolescents diagnosed with ODD do not become violent offenders, and many improve when they receive appropriate intervention and family support (Hawes and colleagues, 2023).

That finding confirmed something I had sensed years earlier. My biggest question looked beyond the diagnosis.

Looking Beyond the Defiance

Cases like Juan Manuel's continued to shape the questions I asked throughout my professional career.

Research describes ODD as a disorder with different developmental pathways. Defiance, emotional dysregulation, and conflict with authority figures are common features of the disorder, but they do not determine a young person's future. A diagnosis should never be used to predict that a child or adolescent will eventually become violent or engage in criminal behavior (Hawes and colleagues, 2023).

That was never my conclusion.

What continued to concern me was the pattern I had observed over time. Cruelty toward animals, repeated bullying, stealing from classmates, manipulation, and an absence of visible remorse suggested that I needed to understand more than the diagnosis recorded in his file.

Many years later, while I wrote my book Dangerous Minds, I realized how often my thoughts returned to Juan Manuel. Despite sharing the same diagnosis, some young people move in very different directions (Castell Britton, 2025).

Around that same period, I became increasingly interested in research on callous-unemotional traits. Those studies encouraged me to ask more careful questions. Some young people show limited empathy, little guilt after causing harm, and a persistent tendency to manipulate or intimidate others. Researchers have emphasized that these characteristics deserve careful assessment and should never be assumed because a child has been diagnosed with ODD (Squillaci and Benoit, 2021).

Looking back, I think Juan Manuel also changed the way I understand schools. Teachers understandably spend much of their time responding to behavior that disrupts learning or places other students at risk. Those decisions have to be made. At the same time, I have often wondered whether schools have enough opportunities to understand the emotional processes developing beneath that behavior before they become even more difficult to change.

The Question Schools Should Ask

I do not know what happened after Juan Manuel left school, or what kind of adult he became. Now and then I catch myself wondering whether someone eventually understood what I had only begun to question all those years ago.

Schools have a responsibility to respond when students become aggressive, intimidate others, or repeatedly violate rules. They also have an opportunity to ask what may be happening long before those behaviors become part of a much larger problem.

When I think about Juan Manuel today, I think about the questions his behavior forced me to ask. Those questions followed me through years of educational and forensic practice, research, and writing, and they continue to shape how I approach young people whose behavior is difficult to understand.

Whenever I meet a student whose actions seem impossible to explain, I remember Juan Manuel. His story reminds me that behavior is often the beginning of the conversation.
